export default "# Xiapu Mudflats: Light, Tide, and Fishing Lines\n\n![Xiapu Mudflats](/images/explore/xiapu-mudflats.svg)\n\nPhotographers call Fujian’s Xiapu coastline a \"living ink painting.\" When the tide recedes, thousands of bamboo poles, nori nets, and reed fences emerge from the South China Sea, creating minimalist lines across the glistening mud. Fine sea mist diffuses sunlight, producing pastel gradients that change by the minute. Villagers continue traditional aquaculture methods that inadvertently craft one of China’s most cinematic landscapes.\n\n## When to Go\n\n- **Peak season:** April–June for seaweed harvests and emerald hills.\n- **Typhoon watch:** Late summer brings dramatic clouds but unpredictable closures.\n- **Golden hours:** 4–6 a.m. and 4–6 p.m. when silhouettes of fishers appear against mirror-like sand.\n\n## Classic Shooting Hills\n\n| Hill | Coordinates | Frame style |\n| --- | --- | --- |\n| Beiqi Hill (北歧) | 26.94°N, 120.12°E | Sunrise silhouettes of workers carrying bamboo poles. |\n| Dongbi (东壁) | 26.89°N, 120.06°E | Sunset reflections with S-curves made by tidal channels. |\n| Xiaohao (小皓) | 26.88°N, 120.17°E | Rolling fog with layered mountains; ideal for long lenses. |\n| Huazhu (花竹) | 26.80°N, 120.01°E | High vantage points to capture full bamboo grids. |\n\nLocal hostels often bundle pre-dawn jeep transfers to these hills so travelers can arrive before tripod crowds.\n\n## Meet the Seaweed Cooperative\n\nXiapu’s economy relies on laver (紫菜) farming. Cooperative leader Lin Meirong explains the choreography:\n\n1. Farmers seed bamboo frames with laver spores in late autumn.\n2. Boats ferry the frames into deeper water during growth phases.\n3. At low tide, crews collect the seaweed sheets, stacking them like emerald quilts.\n4. Solar dryers near the village preserve the harvest for export across China.\n\nTravelers can volunteer for morning harvests; fees support scholarships for fishers’ children.\n\n## Craft and Cuisine\n\n- **Kelp weaving workshops** teach how to braid dried kelp into lampshades—an emerging eco-design export.\n- **Mudflat pantry tours** sample razor clams grilled with garlic, seaweed rice dumplings, and sea-urchin congee.\n- **Village homestays** double as film schools during off-season, where mentors critique landscape portfolios.\n\n## Responsible Photography Guidelines\n\n- Stick to marked ridgelines; stray footsteps crush new kelp shoots.\n- Ask permission before photographing individual workers; many prefer small gratuities deposited into the cooperative tip jar.\n- Use ND filters instead of drone flyovers during bird nesting season (March–May) to avoid disturbing egrets.\n- Share edited photos with the cooperative’s marketing team—they use visitor images in sustainable tourism campaigns.\n\n## Getting There\n\n- **Nearest transport hub:** Fuzhou Changle International Airport (FOC), then a 2.5-hour high-speed rail to Xiapu Station.\n- **Last-mile:** Taxis or private vans reach coastal villages; roads are paved but narrow.\n- **Connectivity:** 5G coverage reached most ridges in 2024, but storms can knock service offline—download offline maps.\n\n## Pairings and Extensions\n\nCombine Xiapu with a cultural detour to Quanzhou’s maritime heritage or hike the volcanic cliffs of Pingtan Island. All three destinations reveal different faces of Fujian: ocean trade, aquaculture artistry, and wind-sculpted geology.\n\n[Back to Explore](/#/explore)\n";
